scenarios.prompt: Arm pain with chest tightness during a session.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Stop all exercise; emergency: call 911 now and stay with the client.

scenarios.prompt: A new lump above the collarbone.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Stop shoulder loading; urgent: urgent care or their primary care provider today.

scenarios.prompt: Shoulder pain that has gotten worse every day this week; no other sign.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Stop shoulder loading for this session; routine referral now: a primary care provider or a physical therapist, without waiting for 2 weeks.

scenarios.prompt: After a fall, the client cannot move the arm.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Stop; emergency: call 911 now; do not move the arm or try to put it back; do not let them drive.
Stop all exercise; emergency: call 911 or go to the emergency department now. This strict mapping is Spindle policy (SAFETY.md, note on infection).

lesson.title: When to refer out
lesson.summary: Referral is a coaching skill: notice, stop, refer to the right place at the right speed, and keep the client training only what is safe.
objectives: Apply the three referral tiers, with the highest matching tier winning.
Use the stop rules and say what to do next.
Know who is outside the base module and how to work alongside a clinician's plan.
Refer in plain, calm, non-diagnostic words, with the right destination and timing.

blocks.content: Every lesson in this module has put a stop-and-refer box beside its screens and progressions. This lesson puts them all in one place. The lists below come straight from Spindle's shoulder safety rules.
A trainer does not diagnose or treat injuries. A trainer notices, stops, and refers. Describe what you see, never name a condition, and never tell a client a screen has cleared them.

content.label: Spindle policy
content.text: Your training is not treatment for a diagnosed condition. A client with diagnosed shoulder pain, or one recovering from surgery, a dislocation or a fracture, trains within the treating clinician's plan, and you do not progress that plan on your own. This is Spindle's rule for trainers, not a research finding.

blocks.content: Which tier: the highest one that matches
Use the highest tier that any sign matches. An emergency sign overrides every urgent or routine sign, and an urgent sign overrides every routine sign.
Emergency: call 911 or go to the emergency department (ER) now

content: Chest pain that feels tight, crushing or squeezing, or chest pain that spreads to the arm, neck or jaw; severe difficulty breathing; the person collapses or does not respond normally

After an injury (a fall, an impact, a joint that "popped out", a seizure or an electric shock), the client cannot move the arm, or the shoulder looks out of place or has changed shape. Do not move the arm or try to put it back. Do not let the client drive themselves.
Signs of a joint infection: the shoulder is suddenly very painful and red or warm, or the client has a fever or feels unwell with shoulder pain

content.label: Note on infection
content.text: A trainer cannot tell whether a joint is infected, and BESS asks for same-day emergency referral when infection is suspected. Spindle's rule is therefore deliberately strict: fever or feeling unwell with shoulder pain goes to the emergency department, not to a same-day appointment. That strict mapping is Spindle policy. A shoulder that feels hot or cold to the touch, or is badly swollen, without sudden severe pain, redness, fever or feeling unwell, stays urgent.

blocks.content: Urgent: urgent care or the client's primary care provider, the same day

content: Sudden or very bad shoulder pain
New loss of active movement without an injury: the client cannot lift or move the arm themselves, even if it can be moved for them

After an injury, pain and weakness, while the arm still moves and the shoulder looks normal (possible acute cuff tear). BESS asks for urgent specialist assessment at the next available clinic; its 2014 guide gives under 2 weeks.
Any other new shoulder pain that started after an injury or accident, such as a fall
The arm or shoulder has changed shape or is badly swollen, with no injury and no sign of infection
Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling in the arm or shoulder
The arm or shoulder feels hot or cold to the touch, with no sign of infection (no sudden severe pain with redness or warmth, no fever, not unwell)
Severe pain in both shoulders
A new lump, mass or swelling around the shoulder
New pain, swelling or stiffness in several joints at once
A child or adolescent with shoulder pain: urgent care or the PCP the same day, for assessment and, if needed, referral to orthopedics; tell a parent or guardian

blocks.content: Routine: a primary care provider or a licensed physical therapist

content: Shoulder pain that is getting worse. Refer now; do not wait for 2 weeks to pass.
Shoulder pain that is not getting worse but has not improved after 2 weeks
Moving the arm or shoulder is very difficult, but the client can still move it themselves
Pain and stiffness that do not go away, including pain that is worse at night
Pain that persists after the trainer has removed the provoking movements

blocks.content: Stop always means no further loading of that shoulder in this session. Changes to range, load or variation belong to a later session, and only if no warning sign remains.

content: Pain comes on or rises with load, or a movement seems to make the shoulder worse - Stop shoulder loading for this session. If the pain is getting worse, routine referral now: there is no need to wait. If it is not getting worse but has not improved after 2 weeks, routine referral.
Numbness, pins and needles, or loss of feeling in the arm or shoulder - Stop. Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling, is urgent.
After an injury, the client cannot move the arm, or the shoulder looks out of place or has changed shape - Stop. Do not move the arm or try to put it back. Emergency.

New loss of active movement: the client cannot lift or move the arm themselves (even if you could move it for them), without an injury - Stop. Urgent. Never treat this as a mobility or control problem to train.
After an injury, pain and weakness, but the arm still moves and the shoulder looks normal - Stop. Urgent (possible acute cuff tear).
Signs of a joint infection: the shoulder is suddenly very painful and red or warm, or the client has a fever or feels unwell with shoulder pain - Stop. Emergency.
Arm pain together with chest pain, tightness, breathlessness, or feeling faint - Stop all exercise. Emergency: call 911.
Pain at night that wakes the client, with stiffness that is not going away - Do not progress shoulder loading. Routine.
Recent injury or accident, such as a fall, with new shoulder pain that has not been assessed - Do not train the shoulder. Use the referral tiers in this lesson.
After shoulder surgery, or a recent dislocation or fracture, still in rehabilitation - Outside the base module. Follow the treating clinician's plan; do not progress it on your own.
Diagnosed neurological condition affecting the arm or neck - Outside the base module.
Diagnosed shoulder condition under current care (for example frozen shoulder, a known cuff tear, instability) - Outside the base module; work only within the clinician's plan.

Children and adolescents with shoulder pain - Outside the base module. Urgent tier: stop shoulder loading, and tell the young person and their parent or guardian to get care the same day, at urgent care or with their primary care provider, for assessment and, if needed, referral to orthopedics. Emergency tier if any emergency criterion applies.
Anyone with a warning sign in the lists in this lesson - Stop and refer.

blocks.content: For subacromial shoulder pain, specialist shoulder guidance from the British Elbow & Shoulder Society lists reassurance among the treatments suitable for primary care: this is usually a self-limiting condition, and most symptoms respond within three months.
That keeps a routine referral calm. It is about one diagnosed condition, and it never delays an urgent or emergency referral.

content: Emergency: call 911 yourself, stay with the client, and do not let them drive. After a fall or impact, do not move the arm or try to put it back. Nothing else happens in the session.

Urgent: "You can't lift your arm yourself today, and that's new. We'll stop the shoulder work now. Please get it checked today, at urgent care or with your primary care provider." Do not offer more training in place of getting help.

Routine, with no other warning sign: "Your shoulder pain is getting worse. Please make an appointment with your primary care provider or a physical therapist now; you don't need to wait." With the shoulder left out, the rest of the session can go ahead if the client feels well.
Every tier: do not name a condition, and do not say it is nothing.

blocks.content: Ask the client to share the plan, ideally in writing. Train within it, ask the clinician before changing it, and do not progress it on your own.

content.prompt: For subacromial shoulder pain, what does specialist shoulder guidance say about how symptoms usually go?
options: It is usually self-limiting, and most symptoms respond within three months
content.explanation: Among the treatments suitable for primary care, the guidance lists reassurance that this is usually a self-limiting condition, and that most symptoms respond within three months.

content.label: What you do first
content.text: For the three urgent red flags below, Spindle's stop rule comes first: leave the shoulder out of today's session and send the client to urgent care or their primary care provider the same day. For anyone under 18, tell a parent or guardian. This is Spindle's rule for trainers; the questions below test only what specialist shoulder guidance says about each sign.

content.prompt: In specialist shoulder guidance, what is shoulder pain in a child or adolescent?
options: A red flag that needs urgent specialist assessment
A routine problem to review if it has not improved after 2 weeks
content.explanation: The guidance lists a child or adolescent with shoulder pain among the red flags that need urgent specialist assessment.

content.prompt: In specialist shoulder guidance, what is a lump or swelling found when someone is assessed for shoulder pain?
options: A routine problem to review if it is still there in 2 weeks
A red flag that needs urgent specialist assessment
content.explanation: The guidance lists swelling or lumps among the shoulder red flags that need urgent specialist assessment.

content.prompt: In specialist shoulder guidance, what is shoulder pain with inflammation in several joints?
options: A routine problem to review if it is not better in 2 weeks
A red flag that needs urgent specialist assessment
content.explanation: The guidance lists inflammation involving several joints among the shoulder red flags that need urgent specialist assessment.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: Pick the tier and say what you do first, who to contact and how soon: (1) arm pain with chest tightness during a session; (2) a new lump above the collarbone; (3) shoulder pain that has gotten worse every day this week, with no other sign; (4) after a fall, the client cannot move the arm; (5) fever and shoulder pain; (6) an ache after training that settled within a day, with no other sign.
